10686.note: This advanced fourth-year course offers an in-depth examination of the dynamic entrepreneurial landscape and intricate ecosystems that support Indigenous business development in Canada. It is designed for students seeking to understand the unique opportunities, challenges, and support structures available to Indigenous entrepreneurs. A special focus will be placed on how entrepreneurial ventures can serve as a powerful means for Indigenous communities to enact their vision, preserve their culture, and address their socioeconomic needs, thereby advancing Indigenous sovereignty and self. Open to non-business students via request for registration form starting on August 1: https://www.uvic.ca/gustavson/undergraduate/minor/index.php

10687.note: Building a revenue profile is essential to accomplishing any organization’s mission – especially when you lead with social/environmental impact. In this course, students will gain perspective on how to foster meaningful collaborations and partnerships with the purpose of building a strong, sustainable revenue profile for your social purpose organization, including for-profits (eg B Corps, co-operatives) and non-profits (eg charities, community organizations). Students will develop business development skills, including how to foster meaningful sales relationships (without “selling your soul”). This course will use the revenue diversification canvas approach to run through types of revenue development, culminating with a strategic financial model that can be employed in their organization. Students will leave with a better understanding on how to strategically build financial impact models for organizations that lead with purpose.

10688.note: Immerses students in the fast-paced world of entrepreneurship. In startup-style teams, students prototype innovative software products using AI, validate markets and solve real customer problems. Guided by founders and industry mentors, students will apply lean startup methods, agile development and human-centered design to build launch-ready ventures. Teams will pitch to investors, demo products and leave equipped to create responsible, high-impact startups and/or innovate inside organizations. Open to non-business students via request for registration form starting on August 1: https://www.uvic.ca/gustavson/undergraduate/minor/index.php

11617.note: Topic description: This course introduces students to political ecology through the lens of contemporary food systems. Food is examined as a socio-ecological infrastructure shaping land use, labour relations, colonial histories, multispecies relations, and environmental outcomes.

11624.note: This is primarily a reading course where we delve deeply into some classic ecology research papers on topics including, but not limited to, the following: the niche, populations, communities, ecosystems, food webs, the rise of experimental ecology, theoretical ecology, conservation biology, meta-analysis, island biogeography, meta-communities, climate change, and neutral theory. We will also examine and discuss the characteristics that make successful research ecologists and research programs. The class will be primarily driven by student discussion and presentations, and is aimed primarily at graduate students and advanced undergraduates.

11626.note: Topics description: Explores the environmental impact of historic and ongoing processes of settler colonialism, with a focus on North America. Draws on political ecology, environmental history, and Indigenous studies to map and analyze how settler political institutions, infrastructure, legal systems, and economies have drastically altered the ecology of Indigenous lands and waters.

11627.note: Topics description: Technology is woven into the fabric of contemporary life. It is pervasive and isolating, transformative and distracting, liberating and crushing. Given its profound impact, it is surprising how little sustained critical attention technology receives. In this course, we will delve into the patterns that shape how technology, including AI, influences social life and relationships with nature. After all, is nature everything that technology is not?

13062.note: Prerequisites: PSYC 201 and PSYC 243. Description: This course examines the psychological processes that shape family relationships across the lifespan. We will explore how families form, function, and change over time, with a focus on core dynamics such as marriage and divorce, parent-child and sibling relationships, communication, conflict, and caregiving. The course also considers how broader social, cultural, and historical contexts influence family life. Drawing on research in family and relationship science, the course emphasizes how psychological principles and empirical evidence can be applied to better understand real-world family relationships and to inform more effective ways of navigating them.
